replacement: 'No, indeed,' I replied, 'it was the same man who told Phoenix. He was a little fellow who never wore shoes, Aristodemus of the deme of Cydathenaeum. He had been at Agathon's feast, and I think that in those days no one admired Socrates more devotedly. I have also asked Socrates about parts of his account, and Socrates confirmed them.' 'Then,' said Glaucon, 'let us have the story again. Is the road to Athens not made for conversation?' So we walked and talked about the speeches on love. And that is why, as I said at the start, I am quite ready to do as you ask, and I will go over them again if you like. For I take the greatest pleasure in speaking about philosophy, or hearing others speak of it, quite apart from the benefit. But when I hear other talk, especially the talk of you rich men and traders, it annoys me, and I pity you, my companions, because you think you are accomplishing something when you are really accomplishing nothing. I suppose you pity me in return, and think me an unfortunate creature, and very likely you are right. But what you merely think about me, I know about you. That is the difference.

COMPANION: I see, Apollodorus, that you have not changed. You are always speaking ill of yourself and of everyone else. I do believe you pity all mankind except Socrates, and yourself first of all. You live up to your old nickname, though I do not know how you got it, Apollodorus the madman, whether or not you deserve it. You are always raging against yourself and everyone but Socrates.
APOLLODORUS: Yes, my friend, and the reason I am called mad and out of my wits is just that I hold these opinions about myself and about you. No other proof is needed.
COMPANION: Enough of that, Apollodorus. Let me ask again that you repeat the conversation.
APOLLODORUS: Well, the story of love went like this. But perhaps I had better begin at the beginning and try to give you the exact words of Aristodemus:

That, or something like it, was the speech of Phaedrus. Some other speeches followed which Aristodemus did not remember, and the next one he repeated was that of Pausanias. Phaedrus, he said, I do not think the subject has been set before us in quite the right form. We should not be called on to praise Love in such an undiscriminating way. If there were only one Love, what you said would be well enough. But since there is more than one Love, you should have begun by deciding which of them we were to praise. I will correct this fault. First I will tell you which Love deserves praise, and then I will try to praise that one in a manner worthy of him. We all know that Love is inseparable from Aphrodite, and if there were only one Aphrodite there would be only one Love. But since there are two goddesses, there must be two Loves. And am I not right that there are two goddesses? The elder has no mother and is called the heavenly Aphrodite, the daughter of Uranus. The younger is the daughter of Zeus and Dione, and we call her the common Aphrodite. The Love who works with her is rightly called common, just as the other is called heavenly. All the gods ought to be praised, but not without distinguishing their natures, so I must try to distinguish the characters of the two Loves. Now actions differ according to the way they are performed.

Take what we are doing now, drinking, singing and talking. These actions are in themselves neither good nor evil. They turn out one way or the other according to how they are done. Done well, they are good, and done wrongly, they are evil. In the same way, not every love is noble and worthy of praise, but only the love that has a noble purpose. The Love who is the child of the common Aphrodite is common in his very nature and has no discrimination. He is the love felt by the lower sort of men, who are apt to love women as well as youths, and who love the body rather than the soul. The objects of this love are the most foolish people, for it desires only to reach its goal and never considers reaching it nobly, so it does good and evil quite indiscriminately. The goddess who is his mother is much younger than the other, and she was born from the union of male and female and shares in both. But the child of the heavenly Aphrodite comes from a mother in whose birth the female has no part. She comes from the male only. This is the love of youths, and since the goddess is older, there is no wantonness in her. Those inspired by this love turn to the male, and delight in the one who is braver and more intelligent by nature. Anyone can recognize the pure enthusiasts of this love by the very character of their attachments.

And the love, more especially, that is concerned with the good, and is perfected in company with temperance and justice, whether among gods or men, has the greatest power. It is the source of all our happiness and harmony, and it makes us friends with the gods above us and with one another. I suppose I too have left out several things that might be said in praise of Love, but I did not do so on purpose. And you, Aristophanes, may now fill the gap or take some other line of praise, for I see that you are rid of your hiccough.

And if we are not obedient to the gods, there is a danger that we shall be split up again and go about in basso-relievo, like the profile figures with only half a nose that are carved on monuments, and that we shall be like tallies. So let us urge all men to piety, that we may avoid evil and obtain the good, of which Love is to us the lord and minister. Let no one oppose him. Whoever opposes him is the enemy of the gods. For if we are friends of the God and at peace with him, we shall find our own true loves, which rarely happens in this world at present. I am serious, and so I must beg Eryximachus not to make fun of this or to see in it any allusion to Pausanias and Agathon, who, I suspect, are both of the manly nature and belong to the class I have been describing. But my words have a wider application. They include men and women everywhere. I believe that if our loves were perfectly fulfilled, and each of us, returning to his primeval nature, had his original true love, then our race would be happy. And if this would be best of all, then the next best thing, under present circumstances, must be the nearest approach to such a union, and that is to find a congenial love.

Here is an excellent proof of her tenderness: she walks not on what is hard but on what is soft. Let us offer a similar proof of the tenderness of Love. He walks not on the earth, nor yet on the skulls of men, which are not so very soft, but in the hearts and souls of both gods and men, which are the softest of all things. In them he walks, and dwells, and makes his home. Not in every soul without exception, for where there is hardness he departs, and where there is softness there he dwells. And since he nestles always, with his feet and in every way, in the softest of soft places, how can he be anything but the softest of all things? Truly he is the tenderest as well as the youngest, and he is also supple in form. If he were hard and could not bend, he could not enfold all things, or wind his way unnoticed into and out of every human soul. A proof of his suppleness and fine proportion is his grace, which everyone admits to be in a special way the attribute of Love, for ungracefulness and love are always at war with one another. The beauty of his complexion is shown by his dwelling among the flowers. For he does not dwell among beauties, of body or soul or anything else, that are bloomless or fading, but in the place of flowers and scents; there he sits and stays. Of the beauty of the god I have said enough, and yet much more remains that I might say.

At his touch everyone becomes a poet, even if he had no music in him before (A fragment of the Sthenoaoea of Euripides.). This too is a proof that Love is a good poet and accomplished in all the fine arts, for no one can give to another what he does not have himself, or teach what he does not know. Who will deny that the creation of the animals is his doing? Are they not all the works of his wisdom, born and begotten of him? And as for the artists, do we not know that only the one whom love inspires has the light of fame? The one whom Love does not touch walks in darkness. The arts of medicine, archery and divination were discovered by Apollo, guided by love and desire, so that he too is a disciple of Love. The melody of the Muses, the metalwork of Hephaestus, the weaving of Athene, and the rule of Zeus over gods and men are also all due to Love, who was their inventor. So Love set the empire of the gods in order, the love of beauty, as is evident, for with deformity Love has no concern. In the days of old, as I said at the start, dreadful deeds were done among the gods, for they were ruled by Necessity. But now, since the birth of Love, and from the Love of the beautiful, every good has sprung up in heaven and earth. Therefore, Phaedrus, I say that Love is the most beautiful and best in himself, and the cause of what is most beautiful and best in all other things. When Agathon had finished speaking, Aristodemus said that there was a general cheer. The young man was thought to have spoken in a way worthy of himself and of the god. And Socrates, looking at Eryximachus, said: Tell me, son of Acumenus, was there not reason in my fears? Was I not a true prophet when I said that Agathon would make a wonderful speech and that I should be in a strait?

No, replied Socrates, consider whether 'necessarily' is not the better word. In my judgment, Agathon, it is absolutely and necessarily true that whoever desires something lacks it, and that whoever desires nothing lacks nothing. What do you think?

'Right opinion,' she replied. 'As you know, it cannot give a reason, so it is not knowledge (for how can knowledge be without reason?). Nor is it ignorance (for ignorance cannot reach the truth). It is clearly something in between ignorance and wisdom.' 'Quite true,' I replied. 'Then do not insist,' she said, 'that whatever is not beautiful is necessarily ugly, or that whatever is not good is evil. And do not conclude that because love is not beautiful and good he must be ugly and evil. He is in between them.' 'Well,' I said, 'surely everyone admits that Love is a great god.' 'Everyone who knows, or everyone who does not know?' 'Everyone.' 'And how, Socrates,' she said with a smile, 'can Love be acknowledged a great god by those who say he is not a god at all?' 'And who are they?' I said. 'You and I are two of them,' she replied. 'How can that be?' I said. 'It is quite easy to understand,' she replied. 'You yourself would admit that the gods are happy and beautiful. Of course you would. Would you dare to say that any god was not?' 'Certainly not,' I replied. 'And by the happy you mean those who possess good and beautiful things?' 'Yes.' 'And you admitted that Love, because he lacks them, desires the good and beautiful things that he lacks?' 'Yes, I did.' 'But how can he be a god if he has no share in what is good or beautiful?' 'He cannot.' 'Then you see that you too deny that Love is divine.'

I said, 'You, stranger woman, speak well. But if Love is as you say, what use is he to men?' 'That, Socrates,' she replied, 'I will try to explain. I have already told you of his nature and birth, and you agree that love is of the beautiful. But someone will ask: of the beautiful in what, Socrates and Diotima? Or rather, let me put the question more clearly: when a man loves the beautiful, what does he desire?' I answered her, 'That the beautiful may be his.' 'Still,' she said, 'your answer raises another question: what does a man get by having beauty?' 'I have no answer ready for what you ask,' I replied. 'Then,' she said, 'let me put the word "good" in place of the beautiful and ask again: if he who loves loves the good, what is it that he loves?' 'The possession of the good,' I said. 'And what does he gain who possesses the good?' 'Happiness,' I replied. 'That is easier to answer.' 'Yes,' she said, 'the happy are made happy by acquiring good things. And there is no need to ask why a man desires happiness. The answer is already final.' 'You are right,' I said.

'Those who are pregnant in the body only turn to women and beget children. This is the character of their love. They hope that their offspring will preserve their memory and give them the blessedness and immortality that they desire for the future. But there are those who are pregnant in soul, for certainly there are men who are more creative in their souls than in their bodies. They conceive what is proper for the soul to conceive or contain. And what are these conceptions? Wisdom and virtue in general. Such creators are the poets and all artists who deserve the name of inventor. But by far the greatest and most beautiful kind of wisdom is the kind concerned with the ordering of states and families, which is called temperance and justice. And when someone has had the seed of these implanted in him from youth, and is himself inspired, he desires on reaching maturity to beget and bring forth.

He wanders about looking for beauty in which he may beget offspring, for in ugliness he will beget nothing. Naturally he embraces beautiful bodies rather than ugly ones. Above all, when he finds a beautiful and noble and well-nurtured soul, he embraces both in one person. To such a person he is full of talk about virtue, and about the nature and pursuits of a good man, and he tries to educate him. At the touch of the beautiful, which is always present to his memory even when the other is absent, he brings forth what he had conceived long before. Together they raise what he has brought forth. They are married by a far closer tie and a firmer friendship than those who beget mortal children, because the children they share are more beautiful and more immortal. Who, thinking of Homer and Hesiod and the other great poets, would not rather have their children than ordinary human ones? Who would not wish to rival them in producing children like theirs, which have preserved their memory and given them everlasting glory? Or who would not want children like those Lycurgus left behind him, the saviors, one may say, not only of Lacedaemon but of Hellas?

Socrates finished speaking, and the company applauded. Aristophanes was about to answer the allusion Socrates had made to his own speech, when suddenly there was a loud knocking at the front door, like a band of revelers, and they heard the sound of a flute-girl. Agathon told the attendants to go and see who the intruders were. 'If they are friends of ours,' he said, 'invite them in. If not, say that the drinking is over.' A little while later they heard the voice of Alcibiades booming in the courtyard. He was very drunk, and he kept roaring and shouting, 'Where is Agathon? Take me to Agathon!' At last, held up by the flute-girl and some of his attendants, he made his way to them. 'Greetings, friends,' he said, standing in the doorway with a thick garland of ivy and violets on his head and ribbons streaming down from it. 'Will you take a very drunken man as a companion in your drinking? Or shall I crown Agathon, which is why I came, and go away? I could not come yesterday, so I am here today, with these ribbons on my head. I want to take them from my own head and crown the head of this most beautiful and most wise of men, if I may call him that. Will you laugh at me because I am drunk? Yet I know very well that I am speaking the truth, even if you laugh. But first tell me: if I come in, will we have the understanding I spoke of (supra Will you have a very drunken man? etc.)?

That is good, Eryximachus, said Alcibiades; and yet it is hardly fair to compare a drunken man's speech with those of sober men. And I should like to know, my dear friend, whether you really believe what Socrates was just saying. I can assure you that the very opposite is true, and that if I praise anyone but him in his presence, whether God or man, he will hardly keep his hands off me.

So he lay down on the couch next to me, the same one on which he had eaten, and no one but the two of us was sleeping in the room. All this can be told without shame to anyone. But what follows I could hardly tell you if I were sober. Yet as the proverb says, 'In vino veritas,' whether with boys or without them (In allusion to two proverbs.); and so I must speak. Nor would I be justified in hiding the lofty actions of Socrates when I come to praise him. Besides, I have felt the serpent's sting; and he who has suffered, as they say, is willing to tell his fellow sufferers only, since they alone are likely to understand him, and will not judge harshly the words or deeds that his agony has wrung from him. For I have been bitten by something worse than a viper's tooth. I have known in my soul, or in my heart, or in some other part, the worst of pangs, more violent in a generous youth than any serpent's tooth: the pang of philosophy, which will make a man say or do anything. And you whom I see around me, Phaedrus and Agathon and Eryximachus and Pausanias and Aristodemus and Aristophanes, all of you, and I need not mention Socrates himself, have experienced the same madness and passion in your longing for wisdom. So listen, and forgive what I did then and what I say now. But let the attendants and any other uninitiated and ill-mannered persons close the doors of their ears.
